chapter_theme: The second half of the plaint to the heart: the heart failed to reach Kailasa, Sivaloka, the Lord of Tillai and Sokkar of Madurai, the Lord ciphered as a pattern of numbers and letters, and the higher light where bindu melts into nada, and is pictured in a run of images of ruin, a tree without a core, a corpse on the stake, a netted deer, a tangled thread, a dog at every eave, a fish that ate poison, an elephant in the jaws, a blind man who threw away his stick, a straw on the waves, wax in the furnace. Against the heart's ego stands a Lord who sold himself to a bard and ate a hunter's leavings.
structure_note: Four-line stanzas continuing the plaint; the address நெஞ்சமே is kept in 662, 664, 666, 667 and 673, while 663, 665, 668, 671 and 672 end in the first person (ஆனேனே, கெட்டேனே) and 669 and 670 in the plural or negative (பிழைத்தோமில்லையே, இருந்தேனில்லையே). 669 opens with a new address, ஊனமூடனே (flawed fool).

662.reading: Without gaining Kailasa, worshipped by all who have cut the darkness that is the rung of the ladder, I, a slave, was dazzled by the things that come to be seen and became like a mango tree without a core, O heart.
662.nuance: ஏணிப்பழு, the ladder-rung, qualifying darkness, is obscure; perhaps the darkness is what the ladder of practice climbs through, or the word is corrupt. ஆணியற்ற மாமரம், a mango tree without its heartwood or peg, is a tree that stands but will not hold. Kailasa is release as a place, as in 661.

663.reading: Not reaching Kailasa, which holds all the worlds in strung light, melting, I this slave took on an alien form, melted within like a flood, and became a corpse set up on the stake.
663.nuance: The first two lines are compressed and may describe the Lord of Kailasa (who protects all the worlds with his light) rather than Kailasa itself. வேற்றுருவப்பட்டு, taking another form, is estrangement from one's own nature. The impaled corpse, கழுவில் இருந்த பிணம், is the harshest of the plaint's self-images.

664.reading: Before the life leaves its station in the body and goes, you did not reach him who ate the leavings of the hunter who drew the bow, but wandered like a deer caught in a net and were tangled like a thread that has lost its end, O heart.
664.nuance: The hunter is Kannappar, who offered Siva meat he had tasted; the Lord who ate his leavings (எச்சில்) is the Lord who accepts love over purity. தலைகெட்ட நூல், a thread with its head lost, cannot be wound.

665.reading: O Father of the Tillai grove whose feet I had taken: I, a dog, spoke sweet words of the waist and gait of lightning-like women with hair on their heads and whole bodies of wickedness, and became a beast that has lost its prey.
665.nuance: The second half of line 3 is read as அடிக்கொண்ட தில்லைவனத்து ஐயனே, நாய் அனையேன்; the printed string allows other divisions. முழுக்குரம்பை, the whole hut, is the body. விடக்கு is flesh or carrion: the beast that lost its meat is the lover left with nothing. Tillai is Chidambaram, the hall of the dance.

666.reading: Not praising the feet of Sokkar of famed Madurai, whom those who live on this earth praise, and not reaching Sivaloka, you wandered and roamed like a dog that puts its head into every house's eave, worthless heart.
666.nuance: சிவலோகம் is the Lord's world, the first of the graded releases. The dog at the eaves (தாவாரம்) answers the market dog of 637; பூவாணர் is read as those who live on the earth (பூ).

667.reading: Not praising the picture that stood matching ten and eight, two fives, thirteen, two and one, you fell into the triple snare that stood set, sowed seed there, and do not know how to let go, O heart.
667.nuance: The numbers are cipher. Tradition reads such counts as tattvas or letter-groups (eighteen, ten, thirteen, two, one as groups of the thirty-six tattvas, or of the mantra-letters), but the verse gives no key; ஓவியம், the picture, is the Lord as the pattern they compose. திரிகண்ணி, the three-stranded snare, is read as the three cravings or the three impurities. வித்திட்டாய், you sowed seed, is begetting or planting the seed of further birth.

668.reading: Not praising the lamp-light that stood supreme, five in form, and three fives and eight as one, and not catching it as fire catches cotton, I wandered like a fish that has eaten poison and was ruined.
668.nuance: அஞ்சு உரு is five in form, perhaps the five letters or the five faces; ஐமூன்றும் எட்டும் ஒன்றாய் (fifteen and eight as one) is cipher without a key here. பஞ்சில் இடு வன்னி, fire put to cotton, is instant catching: the light was there to be taken at once. The poisoned fish continues the hooked fish of 661.

669.reading: Flawed fool: without dying in this earth carrying the perishing worm-nest with pride, we did not go out and escape, as those five who ruled the country left it and went.
669.nuance: பஞ்சவர்கள் ஆண்டிருந்த தேசம் is either the Pandavas' kingdom, left for the forest and the last journey, or the body as the country the five senses ruled. On the second reading the escape is leaving the body's rule, which fits the worm-nest of line 1; on the first it is a renunciation like the Pandavas'. பிழைத்தோம் இல்லையே, we did not escape, is the one plural refrain.

670.reading: This salt-pot that leaks its ooze, this worm-nest that slips away stinking however it tries not to: how could I have desired the glorious city with this? I never withdrew to the land that does not cool.
670.nuance: வீறாம் புரம், the glorious city, is Siva's world; ஆறாத நாடு, the land that does not subside or cool, is obscure, perhaps the unfading land of release or, ironically, this restless world. நாறாமல் நாறி is stinking despite efforts not to.

671.reading: Not praising the supreme flame, the one First that even the rare ones sought and could not know, praised with tenderness, I trusted the dark great life, sank in lust, and became like an elephant caught in the jaws.
671.nuance: அரியவர் அரி தேடி can be read as 'the rare ones' or as Hari (Vishnu) who sought and did not know, the Puranic search for Siva's head and foot. அரிவாயிற் பட்ட கரி is the elephant in the lion's or crocodile's mouth (as in the Gajendra story); கரி can also be charcoal and அரிவாள் a sickle, but the elephant fits the plaint's animal images.

672.reading: Thinking on tantra and setting myself firmly to austerity, thinking on mantra, I grew confused and stumbled, and not seeing the higher light where bindu melts into nada, I became like a blind man who has thrown his stick into the air.
672.nuance: Tantra, tapas and mantra are the practices; what they are for is the light above bindu and nada, the two highest tattvas of Saiva cosmology and of the inner body. The blind man who throws away his stick has lost the one thing that guided him.

673.reading: Not praising him who was sold and became the famed slave of a bard, and who ate the leavings of the hunter with the bow in his hand, you were tossed by egoism like a straw on the waves and melted like wax in the furnace, O heart.
673.nuance: Two acts of the Lord's condescension to devotees: he sold himself into service for a bard (the Madurai sport for the bard Pattiran, or the story of Sundarar's bard), and he ate Kannappar's tasted offering (664). ஆணவம், egoism, is the first of the three impurities; the Lord who stooped is set against the heart that would not.

links.note: 664 names the Lord who ate the hunter's leavings as the one the heart failed to reach; 673 adds his sale to a bard and names the heart's fault as ஆணவம், so the two stories of the Lord's stooping frame the heart's pride.
The plaint opens with the heart as a dog wandering the market and here has it as a dog poking its head under every eave; the first is lust, the second homelessness without Sivaloka.

Arunagirinathar wastes away like a frog that has eaten poison, playing with women who strip his wealth; Pattinathar wanders like a fish that has eaten poison, having missed the light. Both are creatures that swallowed their own death and go on moving.
661 is the kendai fish writhing on the hook of women's maya; 668 is the fish that has eaten poison and wanders. The same fish, caught in the first and dying in the second.

The Kural says that for those bent on ending births even the body is excess; Pattinathar says the escape he failed to make was to leave the country the five ruled, the body, as the Pandavas left their kingdom. Both make leaving the body itself the renunciation that counts.

Sivavakkiyar asks what use a hundred crore Agamas and mantras recited for a hundred crore days are beside the one letter in the heart; Pattinathar says thinking on tantra and mantra left him confused because he did not see the light above bindu and nada. Both put the practice below what it points at.

Tirumular sets bindu and nada above the letters and says the three impurities leave when one stands fierce with SIVAYANAMA; Pattinathar used mantra and tantra and stumbled, because he did not see the light where bindu melts into nada. He does not deny the mantra's power but makes the sight of the light its condition.

The Naladiyar asks whether spices, flowers and finery can remove the body's foulness, which eating strengthens; Pattinathar's body stinks however it tries not to, a salt-pot leaking its ooze. Both say the stink is the body's nature, not a lapse.

source_issues: 662 line 1 ஏணிப்பழுவாம் is obscure and may be corrupt.
665 line 3 (அடிக்கொண்டதில்லைவனத்தையனேநாயனையேன்) can be divided in more than one way; the stanza also lacks the closing address of its neighbours.
663, 665, 668, 671 and 672 end in the first person and 669 and 670 in the plural or negative, where the plaint elsewhere ends நெஞ்சமே.
